tldr: Reuters reports SEC enforcement staff are examining Nvidia's accounting; the stock fell 14%, erasing about $490 billion of value in a day.
The International Court of Justice found Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya; Myanmar's foreign ministry rejected the ruling.
The S&P 500 and Dow closed in correction and the Nasdaq erased its 2026 gain, the worst week for US stocks since April 2025.
The FDA rejected Capricor's Duchenne cell therapy a second time, saying data-integrity problems made its Phase 3 trial unreliable.
Anthropic's $81.3 billion listing is the largest IPO on record; the stock fell about 9% on its second day as AI names sold off.
Fed governor Christopher Waller wants a half-point rate hike in December; futures markets price a quarter point at about 95%.
Mossad's chief pressed Washington to back joint strikes on Iran while US envoys met Qatari mediators in Berlin with no progress.
SpaceX sold $32 billion of Nvidia-chip-backed bonds, the largest tranche pricing at a yield of 8.259%.
The White House replaced national cyber director Sean Cairncross after a week of outages at Microsoft, Chase, Apple and the FAA.
Trump announced a “tremendous tax” on US firms building AI data centers abroad, then said he had not told his own staff.

items.headline: SEC is reportedly examining Nvidia's accounting, and the stock fell 14% in a day
items.body: Reuters reported on Friday, November 20, citing two people briefed on the matter, that SEC enforcement staff are examining potential accounting problems at Nvidia; it could not confirm when the inquiry began or which practices are under review. Nvidia fell 14.01% to close below $130, erasing roughly $490 billion of market value in one session and about $2.7 trillion since October. The SEC declined to comment and Nvidia did not immediately respond. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that the SEC was also examining whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors.
items.plain: Nvidia designs the chips nearly every company training an AI system must buy, which made it the world's most valuable company. The SEC polices whether public companies tell investors the truth about their finances; its staff taking an interest proves nothing, and many such inquiries close with no action. What unsettled investors is the pile-up: Nvidia delayed its quarterly filing, disclosed an internal board investigation, and lost its co-founder as chief executive this month. Two anonymous sources describe the SEC inquiry, so treat it as credible but unconfirmed.
items.why: Index funds made Nvidia one of the largest holdings in most American retirement accounts, so a question about its bookkeeping no longer stays a company story.

items.headline: World Court finds Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya; Myanmar rejects the ruling
items.body: The International Court of Justice ruled nine to six on November 19 that Myanmar breached the 1948 Genocide Convention by committing genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State — the first time the court has found a state responsible for genocide. The judgment, in the case The Gambia filed in 2019, orders Myanmar to pass implementing legislation, prosecute suspects, allow the safe return of displaced Rohingya and report on restitution within two years, with compensation fixed later. Myanmar's foreign ministry rejected the ruling, saying the evidence fell short of the standard of proof and calling the military's 2017 operations “counter-terrorism actions.”
items.plain: The ICJ is the United Nations court that settles disputes between countries; it does not try individuals. In 2017 Myanmar's military drove more than 700,000 Rohingya Muslims into Bangladesh, and the court has now held that the only reasonable reading of the evidence is an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group. The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, but the court has no police force. If Myanmar ignores it, The Gambia's only escalation is the UN Security Council, where China holds a veto.
items.why: A state, not only its commanders, can now be held liable for genocide — the same legal theory South Africa is pressing against Israel over Gaza.

items.headline: S&P 500 and Dow close in correction as the AI trade unwinds
items.body: The S&P 500 fell 3.70% on Friday to 6,910.39, a seventh straight loss that left it in correction territory and down 8.6% for the week, its worst week since April 2025. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.3% to 22,617.73, erasing its gain for 2026, and the Dow fell 1.9% to 48,147.33. Nvidia's 14% decline did most of the damage. Consumer staples was the only S&P sector to finish higher, decliners beat advancers 376 to 123, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell 12 basis points to 4.932%.
items.plain: A “correction” means an index has fallen 10% from its high — a label, not a forecast. Nearly all of this week's damage came from companies tied to artificial intelligence, because those stocks had risen most and are the first thing investors sell to lock in gains or raise cash. Two forces pushed at once: the report of an SEC look at Nvidia's accounting, and expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise rates rather than cut them. Higher rates make profits expected years from now worth less today, which hits expensive stocks hardest.
items.why: With the Nasdaq back to where it started the year, the AI rally has stopped subsidising the rest of the market and started subtracting from it.

items.headline: FDA rejects Capricor's Duchenne cell therapy, saying the trial data cannot be trusted
items.body: The FDA issued a Complete Response Letter on November 20 refusing approval of deramiocel, Capricor Therapeutics' cell therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, saying an inspection found serious deficiencies in the conduct of the Phase 3 HOPE-3 study. The agency said data-integrity problems render the trial's data unreliable and incapable of post hoc remediation, citing unauthorized changes to the statistical analysis plan after the study began and breaches of blinding. It is the second rejection of this application. Chief executive Linda Marbán called the decision “indefensible”; the shares fell roughly 77% to 80% after hours.
items.plain: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a genetic disease that progressively destroys muscle, including the heart, and most patients do not live past their thirties — so there is enormous pressure to approve anything that might help. A Complete Response Letter is the FDA saying no to an application as submitted. The striking part is not that the drug failed to show benefit; the FDA had already said the trial missed its main goals. It is that regulators say the records themselves cannot be relied on, so no reanalysis can rescue them.
items.why: A data-integrity finding, rather than a plain efficacy miss, closes off the usual route of reanalysing existing data and effectively forces a new trial.

items.headline: Anthropic's record IPO is followed by a two-day slide across AI stocks
items.body: Anthropic raised $81.34 billion in its initial public offering, the largest on record, pricing shares at $83 and closing its first day on Thursday at $97.17, up 17%. Valuation figures differ by method, from about $1.28 trillion counting listed shares to roughly $1.76 trillion fully diluted. The stock fell about 9% on Friday as AI and chip names sold off. Investing.com reported that some investors appear to have sold other AI holdings to fund IPO allocations; Capital Economics said the declines have “further to run,” while one fund manager called it profit-taking rather than the end of the AI trade.
items.plain: An initial public offering is the first time a private company sells shares to the public. Anthropic builds AI models and had been privately held, so this listing made it something anyone can buy. A company that large cannot join the market without consequences: index funds have to buy it, and to buy it they sell something else — in practice, other AI stocks. That mechanical selling is part of why a successful debut coincided with a bad week for the sector. Valuations differ because some outlets count only trading shares and others count every share that exists.
items.why: The biggest new supply of AI stock ever created arrived in the same week demand for AI stock thinned, which is a poor sequence for everything already listed.

items.headline: A Fed governor wants a half-point rate hike in December; markets expect half that
items.body: Fed governor Christopher Waller said the central bank should either raise rates half a percentage point at its December meeting or explicitly signal that a quarter-point move will be followed by another in January, telling CNBC the Fed may need to “shock people.” Governor Lisa Cook said policy is not restrictive enough and that waiting risks falling “behind the curve.” October CPI ran hotter than expected and the Cleveland Fed's nowcast puts November headline CPI near 3.9% against a 2% target. CME futures price roughly a 95% chance of a quarter-point hike and 5% for a half point.
items.plain: The Federal Reserve sets the rate banks charge each other overnight, which filters through to mortgages, car loans and savings accounts. It is raising rates rather than cutting them because prices are still climbing faster than its 2% goal. The phrase to watch is “inflation expectations”: if households and businesses treat 3% to 4% inflation as normal, they build it into wages and prices and it becomes self-fulfilling — what officials mean by “unanchored.” Waller's argument is that one loud move now costs less than several quiet ones later. He is one voice on the committee.
items.why: The gap between Waller's half point and the market's quarter point is the gap between a Fed that is believed on inflation and one that is not.

items.headline: Israel presses Washington for new strikes on Iran as US envoys meet Qatari mediators
items.body: Mossad chief Roman Gofman pressed Trump administration officials during a US visit to support joint American-Israeli strikes on Iran, meeting CIA director John Ratcliffe and then envoy Steve Witkoff in Miami, Reuters reported. Witkoff and Jared Kushner met senior Qatari mediators in Berlin on Thursday to discuss a negotiated settlement with Tehran; Axios reported that no progress came of it. Israel's politics are split: Avigdor Liberman said on November 20 that he sees no intelligence justifying a strike now. Accounts of Trump's position conflict — one says he will not decide until the new year, while he told reporters he is not “rushing into anything.”
items.plain: The Mossad is Israel's foreign intelligence service, and its director flying to the United States to lobby for a bombing campaign is the clearest public sign Israel wants America to join one. Qatar acts as a go-between because it talks to both Washington and Tehran, which do not talk directly. The two tracks run against each other: every week of talks that produces nothing strengthens the argument that talking has failed. Note the split inside Israel — a former defence minister saying the intelligence does not support a strike is unusual.
items.why: The live question has shifted from whether Iran's programme justifies a strike to whether diplomacy can produce anything before the case for one wins by default.

items.headline: SpaceX borrows $32 billion against Nvidia chips at more than 8%
items.body: SpaceX sold about $32 billion of bonds on Thursday to finance $47.3 billion of Nvidia GPUs, mostly Rubin-generation processors. The largest tranche, roughly $25.2 billion of Class A3 notes, priced at a yield of 8.259%, against about 5.95% for investment-grade corporate debt that day. The chips are bought by a trust that leases them to SpaceX, keeping the debt off the company's balance sheet; Goldman Sachs and Apollo Global Management led the deal, one piece of a financing package worth more than $40 billion. The Financial Times reported that lenders required none of the chips be used for SpaceX's planned orbital data centers.
items.plain: SpaceX wants an enormous number of AI chips and is borrowing rather than paying cash. The structure is a lease: a separate legal entity owns the chips and rents them to SpaceX, so the debt never appears on SpaceX's own books. Investors demanded about 2.3 percentage points more yield than for ordinary blue-chip debt, and that spread is the price of the risk that AI chips lose value faster than the loan is repaid. The telling detail is the lenders' condition — they would finance chips on the ground but not chips in orbit, where nobody can repossess them.
items.why: AI capacity is increasingly funded with structured debt priced as though the chips backing it are not safe collateral.

items.headline: White House replaces its national cyber director after a week of major outages
items.body: Sean Cairncross is out as national cyber director after about a year, with Pentagon chief information officer Kirsten Davies taking over on an interim basis, two White House officials said. A person close to the White House told Military Times he was fired; a source said Trump believed he “lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job.” The change follows disruptions this month to air travel, banking, communications and government systems, affecting Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, Apple, the FAA and the National Security Agency. An intelligence official said those were separate outages tied to maintenance and technical changes, not a coordinated attack. Trump said of them, “things like that happen.”
items.plain: The national cyber director runs the White House office that writes US cybersecurity policy. It does not operate networks or respond to incidents — that is the job of CISA and the individual agencies. So the official removed after a run of outages was not the official positioned to prevent them, and by the government's own account the outages were not an attack at all, just several large systems breaking in the same week. A permanent successor needs a presidential nomination and Senate confirmation, which takes months.
items.why: The top cyber policy job now sits with an acting official for months, the period Democrats say US defences are already falling behind AI-driven threats.

items.headline: Trump announces a tax on overseas AI data centers, then says he had not told his own staff
items.body: At a White House news conference on Friday, November 20, Trump said American companies building AI data centers abroad would be penalised: “If they want to continue building the centers outside the US, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them.” He cited Google's roughly €13 billion Finnish data-center investment, announced in September. Pressed on the policy, he said, “I haven't even said that to my people.” Bloomberg reported he gave no rate, no timeline and no account of the legal authority; CNBC reported the policy appeared to be news to his own staff. At the same news conference, asked by CNN's Kaitlan Collins whether Vladimir Putin is a friend to the United States, Trump said, “I can't speak to America,” and said people who criticise his relationships with Putin and Xi Jinping are “stupid.”
items.plain: A data center is a warehouse full of computers, and AI companies build them where electricity is cheap and plentiful, which is often not the United States. Trump said he would tax American firms that build them abroad, but a president cannot create a new tax alone — that takes an act of Congress, and he said he had not raised the idea with his own staff. The Putin exchange is separate: he had called Putin a “friend” earlier in the week and drew criticism from both parties, then, offered the chance to call Putin a friend to the country rather than to him, declined to say it.
items.why: An unlegislated tax threat still counts as a planning risk for anyone siting a multibillion-dollar facility, which is how an off-the-cuff remark turns into a real cost.
